subject: Chemistry
description: Solute, solvent, molarity, normality, percentage strength, colligative properties

questions.stem: In a solution of common salt in water, the salt is the:
questions.explanation: Solute = the substance dissolved (smaller quantity). Solvent = the medium that dissolves (larger quantity). Solute + solvent = solution. In salt water, salt = solute, water = solvent. Air is a solution where N₂ is the solvent (78%); O₂, Ar, CO₂ are solutes. Brass is a solid solution of Zn in Cu. The thumb rule — 'more abundant component is the solvent'.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Molarity (M) of a solution is defined as the number of moles of solute per:
questions.explanation: Molarity (M) = moles of solute / litres of SOLUTION (NOT solvent). Easy to prepare in volumetric flask. Drawback: temperature-dependent (volume expands with heat). Compare: Molality (m) = moles of solute / kg of SOLVENT — temperature-independent. Normality (N) = gram-equivalents per litre of solution. Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles. Test trap: 'litre of solvent' is wrong.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: 20 g of NaOH (molar mass 40) dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution gives a molarity of:
questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH = mass / molar mass = 20 / 40 = 0.5 mol. Volume of solution = 500 mL = 0.5 L. Molarity = moles / volume = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1.0 M. Standard formula: M = (w × 1000) / (M.W. × V_mL) = (20 × 1000) / (40 × 500) = 20000/20000 = 1.0.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a colligative property?
questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend ONLY on the NUMBER of solute particles, not their identity. The four classical ones — Relative lowering of vapour pressure (Raoult's Law), Boiling-point elevation, Freezing-point depression, Osmotic pressure. Density depends on the chemical identity / mass of the species — NOT colligative. Real-world uses: salt on icy roads (depresses freezing point); pickle preservation by osmosis; antifreeze in radiators.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given solvent at a particular temperature is called:
questions.explanation: Saturated — exactly at the solubility limit; any more solute will not dissolve. Unsaturated — below the limit (more can dissolve). Supersaturated — beyond the limit; metastable (can suddenly crystallise on disturbance). 'Concentrated' / 'dilute' are non-quantitative everyday terms — not the same as saturated. Solubility usually rises with temperature for solids, falls for gases — why warm beer goes flat fast.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: If 25 g of glucose is dissolved in 75 g of water, the percentage strength (w/w) of the solution is:
questions.explanation: Mass percentage (w/w) = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100 = 25 / (25 + 75) × 100 = 25 / 100 × 100 = 25%. Trap 33.3% would come from dividing by mass of SOLVENT (25/75 × 100), which is wrong. Volume percentage (v/v) is used for liquid solutions of liquids (e.g. ethanol in water).

questions.stem: Why does a saline IV drip use 0.9% NaCl solution rather than pure water?

options.option_text: 0.9% saline is isotonic with blood — pure water would burst RBCs by osmosis
Salt is needed to kill bacteria

questions.explanation: Blood plasma osmolarity ≈ 0.9% NaCl by mass (also called 'normal saline' or 'physiological saline'). If pure water (hypotonic) entered the bloodstream, water would rush INTO red blood cells by osmosis, causing them to swell and burst (haemolysis). Hypertonic solutions would shrivel cells (crenation). Other isotonic IV fluids — Ringer's lactate, dextrose-saline. Real-life application of colligative property — osmotic pressure equality keeps cells stable.
